Stated Claim / Post Context:
'It's quite shocking': Waves are destroying Long Beach's peninsula. It's about to get worse

Long Beach's breakwater protects the shore from waves from the west, but allows waves from the south to hit a narrow stretch of the peninsula that's been badly damaged this year.

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

Long Beach’s peninsula is a narrow spit of land that juts out between Alamitos Bay and the Pacific Ocean. Over the years, its tiny beach cottages were replaced by multistory homes and apartments with sweeping views of the water.

It can seem a precarious spot. But Long Beach residents have long felt protected from the storms of the ocean by a vast breakwater constructed about 80 years ago to give the Navy safe harbor close to shore. The breakwater now serves as protection for Long Beach harbor, one of the largest ports in the world.

Except there is a weakness.

When it was constructed, the breakwater was built far enough east to protect the shore from waves coming from the west, but left a gap that allowed waves coming from the south to hit a narrow stretch of Long Beach‘s Alamitos Peninsula. That means that in the summer, when tropical storms whip up winds and waves traveling north, a small stretch of the peninsula gets the full brunt of those waves.

The result has left the peninsula vulnerable to  the fury of El Niño. Several homes facing the Pacific are being broken apart by months of high surf and powerful waves. The historic wooden boardwalk has splintered. And residents and city officials fear things will get a lot worse as “super El Niño” conditions peak this winter.

This week, the National Weather Service cautioned about beach hazards along the Southern California coast. Newport Beach declared an emergency ahead of the storm and the weather service said strong rip currents and elevated surf could hit south-facing beaches including Long Beach through Thursday afternoon.

“What we’re seeing is new to everyone,” Long Beach Marine Bureau Manager Todd Leland said. “It’s quite shocking, both emotionally and physically.”

What is happening on the peninsula represents a defeat in a decades-old battle against the sea.

For years, the city of Long Beach has managed the battering impact of relentless ocean waves on the exposed tip of the  peninsula by hauling tons of sand to build out a beach that would protect the homes or by piling up sand into a protective berm. For years, it worked — at a cost of more than $1 million per year, the dump-truck loads of sand kept the waves at bay.

This year, that system failed in spectacular fashion, as the remnants of three tropical storms walloped the peninsula back to back, leaving multiple homes falling into the ocean, much of the historic Long Beach boardwalk destroyed, and the seawall exposed for the first time in living memory.

The city has now fast-tracked plans for a moderately more lasting solution to the problem, with hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of sand slated to be dredged up from the bay and deposited along the peninsula’s shoreline. But whether that work will get done in time to protect homes from further damage remains to be seen.

Some peninsula residents have been furious with the city for what they say is a failure to take greater action to protect homes, such as securing funding to install wave-breaking reefs.

“This is a catastrophe of man-made mistakes,” said Kellie Canning, whose house sits on 66th Place, mere feet from homes falling into the ocean. “And the city is nature-washing this.”

California

Few cities in California last week felt the full brunt of the climate crisis more than the small coastal town of San Clemente.

City officials and residents have been warned for years that this type of damage was possible.

A 2015 Long Beach climate resiliency report highlighted the peninsula’s vulnerability to flooding and erosion.

“Given the anticipated rise in sea level and the projected increase in the frequency and severity of storms, continuing to maintain the berm, or even attempts to elevate the berm crest, are not likely to provide sufficient protection,” the report said.

The costs of marine projects must be weighed against the needs of the city as a whole, Leland said, and those costs tend to be high.

To protect the boardwalk and the homes there, the city has been hauling sand from the west end of the beach to the east to create a buffer between the ocean and the shore. The goal, Leland said, is to at least try to replenish the sand as fast as the ocean removes it. That has worked until now, he said.

First, impacts from Hurricane Marie arrived on Labor Day weekend, walloping the coast with 8- to 10-foot waves. Then there was Hurricane Polo, followed by Hurricane Rachel, with each sending higher-than-average waves to shore, Leland said. The cumulative effect has left the city unable to replenish the beach as fast as necessary to protect the homes on the exposed stretch of the peninsula.

“That’s a tipping point,” Leland said. “You lose all capacity to return what was taken.”

The waves seemed to pay the sand no mind the weekend Hurricane Rachel was spinning in the Pacific, with wave after wave bashing ocean-facing homes and sloshing over several collapsed decks as ocean spray covered curious onlookers.

Nature hasn’t been making things easy for the city, U.S. Geological Survey coastal scientist Jonathan Warrick said.

“This summer has been extremely energetic in terms of the waves,” Warrick said. “Because of that, the sand movement has been exceptionally large this summer.”

The city’s effort to replenish the beach has been further stymied by lack of access — because the beach is so eroded, dump trucks can’t go far enough east to drop sand, Leland said.

But even as Long Beach homeowners consider what to do with their wrecked homes, there is a ray of hope for the peninsula, as the city embarks on possibly the largest project to rebuild the beach in as much as 30 years, Leland said.

In August, the City Council gave the green light on a project to dredge the bay to a depth of 20 feet to help ensure ships don’t run aground, according to a September memo written by the city’s director of public works. That project will produce about 415,000 cubic yards of sand that the city will deposit on the peninsula beach, extending it between 100 to 200 feet out from shore, Leland said. Work was expected to start Tuesday.
